extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical mechanics; readers of Newton's Principia
extracted.subtask_description: Derivations and rules governing motion of bodies in a resisting medium where resistance is proportional to the square of velocity (and related geometric/infinitesimal lemmas). Includes propositions, corollaries, examples, and rules for constructing medium density and velocities to make a projectile follow a given curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on applicability of resistance hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Cæterum corpora resisti in ratione velocitatis Hypothesis est magis Mathematica quam Naturalis. Obtinet hæc ratio quamproxime ubi corpora in Mediis rigore aliquo præditis tardissime moventur. In Mediis autem quæ rigore omni vacant ... corpora resistuntur in duplicata ratione velocitatum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish two hypotheses about resistance: (a) resistance proportional to velocity (useful mathematically, approximates reality when motion in stiff media is very slow), and (b) resistance proportional to the square of velocity (applies in media without rigidity). Use the quadratic law for bodies in fluids where the medium offers no 'rigor'; use linear law only as an approximation in very slow motions in stiff media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V (Theor. III): geometric-time progression under v^2 resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpori resistitur in velocitatis ratione duplicata, & sola vi insita per Medium similare movetur, tempora vero sumantur in progressione Geometrica a minoribus terminis ad majores pergente: dico quod velocitates initio singulorum temporum sunt in eadem progressione Geometrica inverse, & quod spatia sunt æqualia quæ singulis temporibus describuntur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance ∝ (velocity)^2 and a body moves only by its initial impulse in a uniform medium, then taking successive times in geometric progression, the initial velocities at those times form an inverse geometric progression and the distances traversed in each of those times are equal. The proof uses hyperbolic ordinates and relations between squares of velocities and their decrements; areas under hyperbola correspond to spaces described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V, Corol. 1: representation of time, velocity, and space via hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: Si tempus exponatur per Asymptoti partem quamvis AD, & velocitas in principio temporis per ordinatim applicatam AB; velocitas in fine temporis exponetur per ordinatam DG, & spatium totum descrip tum per aream Hyperbolicam adjacentem ABGD; necnon spatium quod corpus aliquod eodem tempore AD, velocitate prima AB in Medio non resistente describere posset, per rectangulum AB × AD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperbolic area ABGD to represent space described in a resisting medium over time AD when initial velocity is AB; compare with rectangle AB×AD which represents space in a non-resisting medium with same initial velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V, Corol. 2: ratio of spaces in resistant vs non-resistant medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Unde datur spatium in Medio resistente descriptum, capiendo illud ad spatium quod velocitate uniformi AB in Medio non resistente simul describi posset, ut est area Hyperbolica ABGD ad rectangulum AB × AD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compare space in resistant medium with non-resistant uniform motion, take the ratio of the hyperbolic area to the corresponding rectangle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V, Corol. 3: relating resistance to an equivalent centripetal force and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Datur etiam resistentia Medii, statuendo eam ipso motus initio æqualem esse vi uniformi centripetæ, quæ, in cadente corpore, tempore AC, in Medio non resistente, generare possit velocitatem AB. Nam si ducatur BT quæ tangat Hyperbolam in B, & occurrat Asymptoto in T; recta AT æqualis erit ipsi AC, & tempus exponet quo resistentia prima uniformiter continuata tollere posset velocitatem totam AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a resistance, one may express it as an equivalent uniform centripetal force that would generate velocity AB in time AC in a non-resistant medium; geometrically use the tangent and asymptote construction to find the corresponding time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V, Corol. 4: proportion of resistance to gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Et inde datur etiam proportio hujus resistentiæ ad vim gravitatis, aliamve quamvis datam vim centripetam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the above constructions one can deduce the ratio of medium resistance to gravity or any given centripetal force by the appropriate geometric relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V, Corol. 5: inversion—given resistance proportion to a centripetal force find time and hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: Et viceversa, si datur proportio resistentiæ ad datam quamvis vim centripetam, datur tempus AC, quo vis centripeta resistentiæ æqualis generare possit velocitatem quamvis AB; & inde datur punctum B per quod Hyperbola Asymptotis CH, CD describi debet; ut & spatium ABGD, quod corpus incipiendo motum suum cum velocitate illa AB, tempore quovis AD, in Medio similari resistente describere potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the ratio of resistance to a centripetal force is given, one can determine the time and construct the hyperbola (and thus the space) corresponding to motion under that resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VI (Theor. IV): equal homogeneous spheres under v^2 resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora Sphærica homogenea & æqualia, resistentiis in duplicata ratione velocitatum impedita, & solis viribus insitis incitata, temporibus quæ sunt reciproce ut velocitates sub initio, describunt semper æqualia spatia, & amittunt partes velocitatum proportionales totis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For equal homogeneous spheres moving under resistance ∝ v^2 and driven only by their own initial impulse, if times are taken reciprocally to initial velocities, each describes equal spaces and loses parts of velocity proportional to the whole. The geometric proof uses hyperbolic constructions showing equality of areas (spaces) and proportionality of lost velocity parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII (Theor. V): relation between time, resistance and loss of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora Sphærica quibus resistitur in duplicata ratione velocitatum, temporibus quæ sunt ut motus primi directe & resistentiæ primæ inverse, amittent partes motuum proportionales totis, & spatia describent temporibus istis in velocitates primas ductis proportionalia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If for spherical bodies resistance ∝ v^2 and times are in the ratio: directly as initial motion and inversely as initial resistance, then the parts of motion lost are proportional to the whole and the spaces described in these times are proportional to the product of initial velocities and times. Use the relation that lost parts are proportional to resistance×time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII, Corol. 1: equal-velocity spheres and resistance ∝ diameter^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur si æquivelocia corpora resistuntur in duplicata ratione diametrorum, Globi homogenei quibuscunq; cum velocitatibus moti, describendo spatia diametris suis proportionalia, amittent partes motuum proportionales totis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If equal-velocity spheres experience resistance proportional to the square of their diameters, then homogeneous spheres moving with equal velocities will describe spaces proportional to their diameters and will lose parts of motion proportional to their totals; use mass ∝ diameter^3 and resistance ∝ diameter^2×v^2 to derive the result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII, Corol. 2: resistance in sesquialtered ratio of diameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Si æquivelocia corpora resistuntur in ratione sesquialtera diametrorum: Globi homogenei quibuscunq; cum velocitatibus moti, describendo spatia in sesquialtera ratione diametrorum inverse, amittent partes motuum proportionales totis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance scales as diameter^{3/2}, then for equal velocities, homogeneous spheres will describe spaces inversely proportional in the 3/2 ratio of diameters, still losing motion parts proportional to totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII, Corol. 3: general relation for resistance ∝ D^n
rubrics_metrics.description: Et universaliter, si æquivelocia corpora resistuntur in ratione dignitatis cujuscunq; diametrorum, spatia quibus Globi homogenei, quibuscunq; cum velocitatibus moti, amittent partes motuum proportionales totis, erunt ut cubi diametrorum ad dignitatem illam applicata. ... si resistentiæ sint ut D^n & E^n, spatia ... erunt ut D^{3 - n} & E^{3 - n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General rule: if resistance ∝ diameter^n, then the spaces described (with parts of motion lost proportional to totals) scale as diameter^{3-n}. Use mass ∝ diameter^3 and combine with resistance scaling to get the exponent relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII, Corol. 4: effect of non-homogeneous spheres (density)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quod si Globi non sint homogenei, spatium a Globo densiore descriptum augeri debet in ratione densitatis. Motus enim sub pari velocitate major est in ratione densitatis, & tempus augetur in ratione motus directe, ac spatium descriptum in ratione temporis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spheres are not homogeneous, increase the space described by a denser sphere in proportion to its density; motion under the same velocity scales with density, and time and space scale accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII, Corol. 5: effect of different media
rubrics_metrics.description: Et si Globi moveantur in Mediis diversis, spatium in Medio, quod cæteris paribus magis resistit, diminuendum erit in ratione majoris resistentiæ. Tempus enim diminuetur in ratione resistentiæ, & spatium in ratione temporis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodies in more resistive media traverse less space (all else equal); time and space scale inversely with resistance per the proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma II: moments (fluxions) of generated quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Momentum Genitæ æquatur momentis Terminorum singulorum generantium in eorundem laterum indices dignitatum & coefficientia continue ductis. ... eorum incrementa vel decrementa momentanea sub nomine momentorum intelligo ... generaliter ut dignitatis cujuscunq; A^{n ÷ m} momentum fuerit n ÷ m aA^{(n-m) ÷ m}. ... Genitæ cujuscunq; A^m B^n momentum est momentum ipsius A^m ductum in B^n, una cum momento ipsius B^n ducto in A^m, id est maA^{m - 1} + nbB^{n - 1}; idq; sive integri numeri vel fracti, sive affirmativi vel negativi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma gives rules for infinitesimal increments (moments/fluxions) of algebraic and generated quantities: power rule d(A^n)= n a A^{n-1}, product rule for A^m B^n, reciprocal and root rules, and many worked cases (Cas. 1–6) and corollaries. Use these formulas to compute differential increments of composed geometric/algebraic quantities; they form the foundation for the infinitesimal calculus manipulations used throughout the propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII (Theor. VI): absolute forces in geometric progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpus in Medio uniformi, Gravitate uniformiter agente, recta ascendat vel descendat, & spatium totum descriptum distinguatur in partes æquales, inq; principiis singularum partium (addendo resistentiam Medii ad vim gravitatis, quando corpus ascendit, vel subducendo ipsam quando corpus descendit) colligantur vires absolutæ; dico quod vires illæ absolutæ sunt in progressione Geometrica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the total path in a uniform medium with uniform gravity is divided into equal parts and the absolute forces (gravity ± resistance depending on ascent/descent) at the starts of those parts are taken, those absolute forces form a geometric progression. Use hyperbola-area arguments and relations between small increments of resistance and velocity to deduce proportionality between area elements and velocity, hence the geometric progression of forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII, Corol. 1: representing gravity, velocity and resistance by hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc si spatium descriptum exponatur per aream Hyperbolicam ABNK; exponi possunt vis gravitatis, velocitas corporis & resistentia Medii per lineas AC, AP & AK respective; & vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may represent gravitational force, body velocity, and medium resistance by corresponding straight-line segments associated with a hyperbola whose area represents the space traversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII, Corol. 2: maximum velocity as limit line
rubrics_metrics.description: Et velocitatis maximæ, quam corpus in infinitum descendendo potest unquam acquirere, exponens est linea AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limiting maximum velocity attainable by indefinite descent in the resisting medium is represented by a particular line AC in the geometric construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII, Corol. 3: find maximum velocity from known resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Igitur si in data aliqua velocitate cognoscatur resistentia Medii, invenietur velocitas maxima, sumendo ipsam ad velocitatem illam datam in dimidiata ratione, quam habet vis Gravitatis ad Medii resistentiam illam cognitam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given resistance at some velocity, compute the maximal velocity by taking the mean (in the sense given) between that velocity and a quantity proportional to gravity divided by that resistance—use the geometric mean relations indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII, Corol. 4: expression for infinitesimal time particle
rubrics_metrics.description: Sed & particula temporis, quo spatii particula quam minima NKLO in descensu describitur, est ut rectangulum KN × PQ. ... Ergo particula temporis est ut KN × PQ, vel quod perinde est, ut PQ ÷ CK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An infinitesimal time element for the small space NKLO is proportional to KN×PQ (and equivalently PQ/CK); use this when integrating or composing small area/time/velocity relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII, Corol. 5: ascending time particle analogous
rubrics_metrics.description: Eodem argumento particula temporis, quo spatii particula nklo in ascensu describitur, est ut pq ÷ Ck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ascent, the infinitesimal time element corresponding to a small space is analogously pq/ Ck; apply symmetry to ascent/descent constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX (Theor. VII): sectors as time measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Positis jam demonstratis, dico quod si Tangentes angulorum sectoris Circularis & sectoris Hyperbolici sumantur velocitatibus proportionales, existente radio justæ magnitudinis: erit tempus omne ascensus futuri ut sector Circuli, & tempus omne descensus præteriti ut sector Hyperbolæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the tangents of circular and hyperbolic sectors are taken proportional to velocities (with a suitable radius), then the total future ascent-time corresponds to the area (sector) of a circle and the past descent-time to the sector of a hyperbola. Use the infinitesimal-partition argument comparing sectoral elements and triangle elements to equate sectoral measures with time increments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX, Case 1 and Case 2 (sectoral particle-time equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case 1: sector particle tDv corresponds to infinitesimal time pq/ Ck; Case 2: hyperbolic sector particle TDV corresponds likewise to PQ ÷ CK; composing gives whole sector proportional to whole time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two small-area arguments (comparing triangular and sectoral infinitesimals) show that sector elements equal corresponding infinitesimal times; summing yields the sector-time equivalence for whole ascent/descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX, Corol. 1: relation of areas and spaces in fall
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc si AB æquetur quartæ parti ipsius AC, spatium ABRP, quod corpus tempore quovis ATD cadendo describit, erit ad spatium quod corpus semisse velocitatis maximæ AC, eodem tempore uniformiter progrediendo describere potest, ut area ABRP ad aream ATD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate the area representing actual space described under resistance to the sector area representing time; use these to compare motion in resisting vs non-resisting media for specified proportions of the maximal velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX, Corol. 2–5: further relations of space/time/velocity via sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol.2: analogous result for ascent. Corol.3: velocity at time ATD in medium with resistance is to the velocity it would acquire in non-resistant medium as triangle APD to hyperbolic sector ATD. Corol.4: analogous for ascent (ApD to AtD). Corol.5: times for acquiring or losing velocities correspond to ratios of sector to triangle or arc to tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triangle vs sector (circular/hyperbolic) area comparisons to compute instantaneous and comparative velocities in resisting and non-resisting media and to relate acquisition/loss times to geometric sector/triangle ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX, Corol. 6–7: given time -> given space and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol.6: From a given time one can determine the space of ascent or descent. Corol.7: Conversely, from a given ascent/descent space one determines the times ADt or ADT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the established correspondences (sector↔time, area↔space) to invert between space and time quantities for motion in a resisting medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X (Prob. III): determining medium density and velocities for a given curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendat uniformis vis gravitatis directe ad planum Horizontis, sitq; resistentia ut medii densitas & quadratum velocitatis conjunctim: requiritur tum Medii densitas in locis singulis, quæ faciat ut corpus in data quavis linea curva moveatur, tum corporis velocitas in iisdem locis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a desired trajectory ACK and resistance law R ∝ density × v^2, determine both the required medium density distribution and the body velocities at each point so that a projectile will follow the given curve (i.e., make progress and regression velocities equal at the same points). The method constructs small perpendiculars and tangent relations, uses infinitesimal line elements, and derives expressions for density in terms of geometry (e.g., CF, FG, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, core relation for medium density
rubrics_metrics.description: Et inde resistentia fit ut HF directe & FG inverse, sive ut HF ÷ FG. ... Velocitas autem ut descripta longitudo CF directe & tempus [sqrt]FG inverse, hoc est ut CF ÷ [sqrt]FG, adeoq; quadratum velocitatis ut CFq. ÷ FG. Quare resistentia, ipsiq; proportionalis {Cf - CF} ÷ FG est ut Medii densitas & ut CFq. ÷ FG conjunctim; & inde Medii densitas ut {Cf - CF} ÷ FG directe & CFq. ÷ FG inverse, id est ut {Cf - CF} ÷ CFq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From infinitesimal geometric relations one obtains density ∝ (Cf - CF) / CF^2 (after substitutions), giving a local formula for medium density required to make the body follow the curve at that point. Use tangent/normal and small-element relations to compute these quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Corol. 1–2: explicit algebraic forms for density and resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol.1: if in Cf capiatur Ck æqualis CF ... Medii densitas fiet ut {FG - kl} ÷ {CF × {FG + kl}}. Corol.2: hence with substitutions the ratio resistentia ad gravitatem is given as a certain rectangle formula (CF × (FG - kl) ÷ 4FG^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided algebraic substitutions (CF, FG, kl, etc.) and series expansions to obtain explicit rational expressions for local medium density and the ratio of resistance to gravity at each point on the curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Corol. 3: solving the problem via series expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Et hinc si curva linea definiatur per relationem inter basem seu abscissam AB & ordinatim applicatam BC; & valor ordinatim applicatæ resolvatur in seriem convergentem: Problema per primos seriei terminos expedite solvetur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the curve is given by an analytic relation y(x) whose ordinate admits a convergent series expansion, then solve the problem by taking the first few terms of the series; interpret the first term as the ordinate at start, the second term as the small tangent difference, the third as curvature, etc., to obtain approximations for density and velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Exempl. 1 (semicircle): density for circular arc trajectory
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempl.1: Sit Linea ACK semicirculus ... Deducendo ... prodit Medii densitas ut a ÷ ne, hoc est (ob datam n) ut a ÷ e seu OB ÷ BC, id est ut Tangentis longitudo illa CT ... & resistentia erit ad gravitatem ut a ad n ... corpus illud describet circuli quadrantem LCK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a semicircular trajectory one finds medium density proportional to the tangent length CT (OB/BC) and resistance-to-gravity ratio proportional to OB:OK; thus selecting the density accordingly makes the projectile describe a circular quadrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Exempl. 2 (parabola): no finite density yields parabola in resisting medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempl.2: Sit linea ALCK Parabola ... Null a igitur Medii densitate movebitur Projectile in Parabola, uti olim demonstravit Galilæus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A parabola cannot be the trajectory of a projectile in any uniformly resisting medium where resistance ∝ density × v^2; this reproduces Galileo's result that parabolic motion is characteristic of vacuum or non-resisting media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Exempl. 3 (hyperbola): density reciprocity with tangent length
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempl.3: Sit linea AGK Hyperbola ... Ponatur itaq; quod Medii densitates in locis singulis G sint reciproce ut distantiæ XY, quodq; resistentia in loco aliquo G sit ad Gravitatem ut XY ad YG; & corpus de loco A justa cum velocitate emissum describet Hyperbolam illam AGK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For certain hyperbolic trajectories one obtains medium density inversely proportional to a certain tangent-length XY, and resistance ratios tied to XY and YG; selecting density = 1/XY yields the designed hyperbola path with appropriate initial velocity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Exempl. 4 (general hyperbola family): series method and density formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempl.4: Ponatur ... Hyperbola sit ... VG reciproce ut ipsius ZX vel DN dignitas aliqua ND^n ... Resolvatur terminus ... et inde Medii densitas S ÷ {R × [sqrt]{1 + QQ}} ... Resistentia autem in eodem loco G fit ad Gravitatem ut S in XY ÷ A ad 2RR ... Velocitas ibidem ea ipsa est quacum corpus projectum in Parabola pergeret ...  Q. E. I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a hyperbola defined by parameters leading to VG ∝ 1/DN^n, expand VG in a convergent series and map coefficients Q,R,S to obtain a general density expression S/(R sqrt(1+Q^2)); use the series coefficients to derive local density/resistance formulas for the trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on hyperbolic-type trajectories and practical approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoniam motus non fit in Parabola nisi in Medio non resistente, in Hyperbolis vero hic descriptis fit per resistentiam perpetuam; perspicuum est quod linea, quam Projectile in Medio uniformiter resistente describit, propius accedit ad Hyperbolas hasce quam ad Parabolam. ... Ipsæ vero in usum sic deducentur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trajectories in a uniformly resisting medium are of a hyperbolic type and are closer to the hyperbolas described here than to parabolas; in practical applications those hyperbolic approximations are useful. Use tangent-based density inverses (reciprocal of tangent length) as practical density prescriptions for achieving given hyperbolic trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X, Regulations (Reg. 1–3): invariance and scaling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Reg.1: Si servetur Medii densitas in A & mutetur angulus NAH, manebunt longitines AH, AI, HX. Reg.2: Si servetur tum angulus NAH tum Medii densitas in A, & mutetur velocitas quacum corpus projicitur; servabitur longitudo AH, & mutabitur AI in duplicata ratione velocitatis reciproce. Reg.3: Si tam angulus NAH quam corporis velocitas in A, gravitasq; acceleratrix servetur, & proportio resistentiæ in A ad gravitatem motricem augeatur in ratione, ... Augetur vero proportio resistentiæ ad pondus, ubi vel gravitas specifica sub æquali magnitudine fit minor, vel Medii densitas major, vel resistentia, ex magnitudine diminuta, diminuitur in minore ratione quam pondus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules for design/variation: (1) holding density at A and changing the launch angle preserves certain baseline lengths (AH, AI, HX) allowing hyperbola determination; (2) holding angle and density at A while changing launch speed keeps AH fixed, while AI changes inversely as square of speed; (3) holding angle, speed, and gravitational acceleration while increasing the local resistance-to-motive-gravity ratio changes AH and AI in specified proportions—account for density, specific gravity, and size when adjusting resistance-to-weight ratios.
